titulo: Who's arriving: bots by purpose and signed agents (the concept)
lead: Not every AI bot that visits your site does the same thing: some index for search, others read when a person asks, others collect for training. The robots.txt file asks by purpose, but it doesn't prove who is who. In this lesson you read your robots.txt by purpose and learn what the Web Bot Auth draft proposes for identifying the agent.
objetivo: read your robots.txt by purpose and understand why only a signature on the request identifies the agent.

aprende.t: Search, user action and training: three purposes
The robots.txt as read by the kit's robots.py
Why the name in the User-Agent proves nothing
Web Bot Auth and signed agents, as a concept

hero_alt: The front door of a workshop at night, with a lit badge reader and an industrial humanoid robot standing in front of it.

secoes.titulo: Who knocks at the door, and how to tell

nos.detalhe: They build the index that answers use. Blocking usually takes your site out of that AI's search answers. The full decision is in the inemaSEO Program.
They visit the page when a person asks the assistant to read or open the address. This is the closest thing to an agent acting on someone's behalf.
They collect text to train models. Allowing or blocking is a business decision; blocking training does not remove you from search.

The robots.txt is a request, and the name in the User-Agent can be forged. The Web Bot Auth draft proposes that the agent sign the request (HTTP Message Signatures, RFC 9421) and publish its keys; the site checks them. It is still a draft at the IETF.

secoes.legenda: Purpose is decided in robots.txt; identity only with a signature. Security in depth for this is course 4.

texto: One group per User-agent with Allow and Disallow. Bots that follow the rule respect it; the CDN or firewall is what enforces it.
Write the decision by purpose and note the reason in a comment. The full step-by-step is in lesson 6 of the inemaSEO Foundation course.
Each bot introduces itself by name in the User-Agent header. It's just text: any program can write "GPTBot". It's good for statistics, not for trust.

In the draft-ietf-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol draft (Sept/2026, Cloudflare and Google, an IETF working group document, not yet an RFC), the agent signs the request and sends the Signature-Agent header; the keys live in a JWKS directory at a well-known URI.
On Cloudflare, since 07/01/2026, signed agents count as Verified, with the field "Direct versus Intermediary access".

exemplo.texto: Nothing to install in this course. Knowing it exists helps you read your CDN dashboard and not trust a bot's name alone.

secoes.sub: The robots.py reads a robots.txt (file or URL) and tells you, by purpose, who can get into the root of the site. Simplified rule: only the root "/"; partial = blocks some paths.

perguntas.p: A person pastes your site's link into the assistant and asks for a summary. What kind of bot reads the page?
opcoes: A training bot, like OpenAI's GPTBot
A search bot, like Microsoft's Bingbot
None: the assistant doesn't actually access sites
perguntas.explica: User-action bots visit the page at someone's request. Blocking them stops the assistant from reading your site even when the customer asks.

perguntas.p: Your log shows User-Agent "GPTBot". Does that prove it was OpenAI?
opcoes: No: the User-Agent is text anyone can write
Yes: the browser doesn't let that name be faked in the header
Yes, if the site's robots.txt allows GPTBot
No, because GPTBot is a search bot, not a training bot
perguntas.explica: The name declares, it doesn't prove. Proof comes from a signature on the request (Web Bot Auth, draft) or from the verification the CDN does.

perguntas.p: What does the Web Bot Auth draft propose?
opcoes: A new field in robots.txt with a password for each bot
That the site register WebMCP tools for each bot
Blocking all agents by default on the CDN
Have the agent sign the request and the site verify it
perguntas.explica: HTTP signature (RFC 9421), the Signature-Agent header, and keys in a JWKS directory at a well-known URI. An IETF draft, not an RFC.

perguntas.p: The robots.txt allows everything, but an agent can't read the site. Where do you look first?
opcoes: In llms.txt, which says who can read the site
In the CDN dashboard: it enforces; robots.txt only asks
In the origin trial token published in the page's meta tag
In the MCP server that serves the agents
perguntas.explica: What really blocks is the CDN or the firewall. If the dashboard blocks what robots.txt allows, the dashboard wins.

itens.texto: Search, user action, and training: decide one by one.
robots.txt asks, User-Agent declares, the CDN enforces.
Web Bot Auth signs the request; it's still a draft.
